title: What is CREC and How Does It Shape Pete Hegseth’s Religious Rhetoric?
author: Samuel Perry
content:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s conservative evangelical religious beliefs
[drew attention even before his confirmation
hearings](https://theconversation.com/why-the-religious-beliefs-of-trump-
defense-pick-pete-hegseth-matter-245601) in January 2025. He is a member of
the Communion of Reformed Evangelical Churches – CREC – whose beliefs have
been influenced by a 20th-century movement called [Christian
Reconstructionism](https://theconversation.com/what-is-christian-
reconstructionism-and-why-it-matters-in-us-politics-266915).

Many CREC leaders call for the implementation of biblical law and a
[theocratic state](https://canonpress.com/products/the-case-for-christian-
nationalism) structured on [Christian
patriarchy](https://tucson.com/news/nation-world/government-
politics/article_93c002eb-9598-5740-9c8f-82a2057b1a4f.html). Theocratic states
are ruled according to religious laws, which in the case of the CREC means a
conservative evangelical understanding of Christianity.

The [CREC website](https://crechurches.org) claims to have over 160 churches
and parishes spread across North America, Europe, Asia and South America.

Hegseth’s [use of religious language and
prayers](https://www.npr.org/2026/03/31/nx-s1-5739333/in-pentagon-briefings-
hegseth-leans-into-religious-rhetoric) has raised questions about his
religious beliefs in relation to his role as secretary of defense. At a prayer
service on March 25, 2026, during the current war in Iran, Hegseth said, “Let
every round find its mark against the enemies of righteousness and our great
nation.” [He went on to add](https://www.theguardian.com/us-
news/2026/mar/26/hegseth-prayer-violence-pentagon): “Give them wisdom in every
decision, endurance for the trial ahead, unbreakable unity, and overwhelming
violence of action against those who deserve no mercy.”

As a [scholar of the Christian right](https://honors.baylor.edu/person/samuel-
perry-phd), I have studied [the
CREC](https://www.libertymagazine.org/article/looking-for-a-holy-war). To
understand Hegseth’s rhetoric, it is helpful to understand what the CREC is
and its controversial leadership.

**What is the CREC?**

The CREC church is a network of churches across the globe. It is associated
with the congregation of Doug Wilson, [the pastor who founded Christ
Church](https://www.npr.org/transcripts/1224382120) in Moscow, Idaho. Christ
Church is the flagship church of the CREC and operates as a denominational
headquarters. Wilson grew up in the town, where his father was an evangelical
minister.

[Wilson co-founded the CREC](https://theconversation.com/in-moscow-idaho-
conservative-christian-reconstructionists-are-thriving-amid-evangelical-
turmoil-162652) in 1993 and is the public figure most associated with the
network of churches. Christ Church operates as the hub for Logos Schools,
Canon Press and New Saint Andrews College, all located in Moscow.

Logos is a set of private schools and homeschooling curriculum; Canon Press is
a publishing house and media company; and New Saint Andrews College is a
university. All of these were founded by Wilson and associated with Christ
Church. All espouse the view that Christians are at odds with – or at war with
– secular society.

While he is not Hegseth’s pastor, [Wilson is the most influential
voice](https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2025/05/23/doug-wilson-new-
right-pastor-hegseth-trump-officials-00355376) in the CREC, and the two men
have spoken approvingly of one another.

Hegseth invited Wilson to give a prayer service at the Pentagon in February
2026. Wilson [told the assembled military members](https://dougwils.com/books-
and-culture/s7-engaging-the-culture/remarks-at-the-pentagon-prayer-
meeting.html), “If you bear the name of Jesus Christ, there is no armor
greater than that. Not only so, but all the devil’s R&D teams have not come up
with armor-piercing anything.” In other words, Wilson tied the success and
safety of military members and their missions to a belief in Jesus Christ and
the military’s enemies as agents of the devil.

As Wilson steadily grew Christ Church in Moscow, Idaho, he and its members
sought to [spread their message by making Moscow a conservative
town](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2021/nov/02/christ-church-idaho-
theocracy-us-america) and establishing churches beyond it. Of his hometown,
Wilson [plainly states](https://www.spokesman.com/stories/2019/nov/17/leaders-
of-moscows-christ-church-say-theyre-pushin/), “Our desire is to make Moscow a
Christian town.”

The CREC doctrine is opposed to religious pluralism or political points of
view that diverge from its theology. On its [website, the CREC
says](https://crechurches.org/story/) it is “committed to maintaining its
Reformed faith, avoiding the pitfalls of cultural relevance and political
compromise that destroys our doctrinal integrity.”

CREC churches adhere to a [highly
patriarchal](https://www.sonsofpatriarchy.com) and conservative interpretation
of Scripture. Wilson has said that in a [sexual
relationship](https://www.vice.com/en/article/disobedient-women-book-excerpt-
ohio-churches-abuse/), “A woman receives, surrenders, accepts.”

**Church-state separation**

In a broader political sense, CREC theology includes the belief that the
establishment clause of the Constitution [does not require a separation of
church and state](https://idahocapitalsun.com/2024/07/05/new-extremely-
american-podcast-tackles-christian-nationalism-through-story-of-an-idaho-
town/). The most common reading of the [establishment
clause](https://constitution.congress.gov/browse/essay/amdt1-2-1/ALDE_00013267/)
is that freedom of religion prohibits the installation of a state religion or
religious tests to hold state office.

According to scholar of religion [Julie
Ingersoll](https://webapps.unf.edu/faculty/bio/N00002560), in this religious
community there is “[no distinction between religious issues and political
ones](https://theconversation.com/why-the-religious-beliefs-of-trump-defense-
pick-pete-hegseth-matter-245601).”

The CREC broadly asserts that the government and anyone serving in it should
be Christian. For Wilson, this means [Christians and only Christians are
qualified to hold political
office](https://www.npr.org/podcasts/510381/extremely-american) in the United
States.

**‘Church planting’**

Scholar of religion Matthew Taylor [explained in an interview with the
Nashville
Tennessean](https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/elections/2025/01/13/pete-
hegseth-nomination-is-milestone-for-doug-wilsons-church-
movement/76947642007/), “They believe the church is supposed to be militant in
the world, is supposed to be reforming the world, and in some ways conquering
the world.”

While the CREC may not have the name recognition of some large evangelical
denominations or the visibility of some megachurches, it boasts churches
across the United States and internationally.

Like some other evangelical denominations, the CREC uses “[church
planting](https://crechurches.org/church-planting/)” to grow its network.
Planted churches do not require a centralized governing body to ordain their
founding. Instead, those interested in starting a CREC congregation contact
the CREC. The CREC then provides materials and literature for people to use in
their church.

**CREC controversies**

As the church network has grown, it has drawn attention and scrutiny. In 1996,
Wilson published a book [positively depicting
slavery](https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/americas/us-politics/pete-
hegseth-pastor-slavery-south-b2704592.html) and claiming slavery cultivated
“affection among the races.”

Accusations of [sexual abuse](https://www.vice.com/en/article/inside-the-
church-that-preaches-wives-need-to-be-led-with-a-firm-hand/) and the church’s
handling of it have also brought national news coverage. Vice media’s Sarah
Stankorb [interviewed](https://www.vice.com/en/article/inside-the-church-that-
preaches-wives-need-to-be-led-with-a-firm-hand/) many women who talked about a
culture, [especially in marriage](https://www.yahoo.com/news/pete-hegseths-
mother-begged-him-110005827.html), where sexual abuse and assault was common.
That reporting led to a [podcast that details the accounts of
survivors](https://www.sonsofpatriarchy.com). [In
interviews](https://www.npr.org/podcasts/510381/extremely-american), Wilson
has denied any wrongdoing and said that claims of sexual abuse would be
directed to the proper authorities.

Hegseth’s actions in May and June of 2025 as secretary of defense concerning
gender identity and [banning trans
people](https://www.washingtonpost.com/national-
security/2025/05/08/transgender-troops-hegseth-trump-supreme-court/) from
serving in the military, in addition to [stripping gay activist and politician
Harvey Milk’s](https://www.npr.org/2025/06/04/nx-s1-5422936/hegseth-harvey-
milk-navy-ship-name) name from a Navy ship, brought more attention to the
CREC.

**Hegseth’s religious rhetoric**

As the Trump administration engages in military conflicts around the globe,
Hegseth often uses religious language to justify them.

[In a March 5, 2026,
speech](https://www.war.gov/News/Speeches/Speech/Article/4424673/remarks-by-
secretary-of-war-pete-hegseth-at-the-americas-counter-cartel-confere/) to
South American and Central American leaders, Hegseth justified intervention in
Venezuela, the blockade of Cuba and the attacks on boats across the region by
invoking a shared Christian identity.

Hegseth said, “We share the same interests, and, because of this, we face an
essential test – whether our nations will be and remain Western nations with
distinct characteristics, Christian nations under God, proud of our shared
heritage with strong borders and prosperous people, ruled not by violence and
chaos but by law, order, and common sense.”

Hegseth’s comments about Iran since bombing began on Feb. 28 have also invoked
religion. Some of these invocations align with Hegseth’s recurring references
to the [Crusades in the Middle
Ages](https://www.history.com/articles/crusades) – a centuries-long holy war
between Christians and Muslims. Hegseth [has a
tattoo](https://nymag.com/intelligencer/article/iran-pete-hegseth-holy-
war.html) that says “Deus Vult” – “God wills it” – the rallying cry of
Crusaders, another with the Arabic word for infidel, and the Jerusalem cross,
a prominent Christian nationalist symbol. He also published a book titled
“American Crusade.”

In framing the use of overwhelming force in Iran, [Hegseth
said](https://www.rev.com/transcripts/hegseth-60-minutes-interview), “We’re
fighting religious fanatics who seek a nuclear capability in order for some
religious Armageddon.”

As long as Hegseth remains the secretary of defense, his affiliation with the
CREC and religious language will likely provide insight into how these
conflicts are managed at home and abroad.
